How to Brew Your First Beer at Home

Brew your first batch step by step, from equipment and sanitation to fermentation, bottling and the measurements that matter most.

Updated 2026-07-28 · 21 min read

What you will learn

  • Prepare the essential equipment and ingredients before brew day.
  • Understand how wort becomes beer from the boil through fermentation.
  • Separate cleaning from sanitizing to protect the batch.
  • Track a few useful measurements without overcomplicating your first brew.

In this guide

  1. Plan a first batch you can finish confidently
  2. Brew your first beer in eight clear steps
  3. Gather the equipment and four core ingredients
  4. Clean first, then sanitize
  5. Follow the brew-day sequence
  6. Let fermentation work
  7. Record the measurements that matter
  8. Avoid common first-batch mistakes
  9. Taste, record and improve the next batch

Plan a first batch you can finish confidently

Your first batch is mainly about learning the complete sequence: prepare, brew, cool, ferment and package. Choose a short, well-documented recipe and read it from beginning to end before heating any water.

Check the ingredients, equipment and time you need. Mark every point where the recipe asks for a temperature, volume, hop addition or gravity reading so you are not searching for tools while the wort is hot.

A sensible first recipe

An extract kit or a simple all-grain recipe with few ingredients reduces decisions. Finishing every stage cleanly and taking notes matters more than controlling every advanced variable.

Brew your first beer in eight clear steps

The complete beginner brewing sequence

Use this sequence as your high-level map. Your recipe supplies the exact quantities, temperatures and timings for the beer you are making.

  1. 01

    Read the recipe and prepare the equipment

    Check every ingredient, vessel and measurement before heating water. Clean reusable equipment, then prepare sanitizer according to its label.

    Review the equipment and ingredients
  2. 02

    Produce the sweet wort

    Dissolve malt extract as directed or mash crushed malt so enzymes can convert starch into sugars. Follow one method and one recipe consistently.

    Understand wort
  3. 03

    Boil the wort and add hops on schedule

    Maintain the recipe’s boil and make each hop addition at its specified time. Earlier and later additions serve different bitterness and aroma purposes.

    Learn hop timing and bitterness
  4. 04

    Cool the wort and protect the cold side

    After the boil, cool the wort toward the yeast’s pitching range. Every surface touching cooled wort must already be clean and properly sanitized.

    Apply the cold-side sanitation rule
  5. 05

    Transfer safely and measure original gravity

    Move the cooled wort into the sanitized fermenter, measure OG when the recipe requires it, and record the reading without returning the sample.

    Use OG and FG correctly
  6. 06

    Pitch healthy yeast and control fermentation

    Add the yeast within its recommended temperature range, close the fermenter and keep it stable. Avoid opening it merely to check airlock bubbles.

    Follow fermentation safely
  7. 07

    Confirm completion before packaging

    Respect the recipe timeline and confirm stable final gravity when instructed. Bottle or keg only after fermentation is complete, using a measured carbonation method.

    Check before packaging
  8. 08

    Condition, taste and improve

    Give the packaged beer the required conditioning time, then taste it alongside your recipe and brew notes. Record one success and one change for the next batch.

    Build a useful tasting note

Gather the equipment and four core ingredients

The exact setup depends on your method, but most first batches need a suitable kettle, a thermometer, a fermenter and airlock, transfer equipment, packaging equipment and a way to measure volume. Your recipe may also call for a hydrometer, grain bag or wort chiller.

Beer starts with water, malt, hops and yeast. Water forms the batch, malt or malt extract provides fermentable sugars, hops add bitterness and aroma, and yeast turns wort sugars into alcohol, carbon dioxide and flavor compounds.

Wort

The sweet liquid produced from malt before fermentation. Once yeast ferments it, wort becomes beer.

In the homebrewing glossary: Wort.

Clean first, then sanitize

Cleaning removes residue and visible soil. Sanitizing treats an already clean surface to reduce microorganisms that could spoil the beer. Sanitizer cannot compensate for equipment that is still dirty.

After the boil, anything touching cooled wort or beer must be clean and properly sanitized: the fermenter, lid, thermometer, tubing, hydrometer jar and packaging equipment. Follow the product label for concentration, contact time and rinsing.

The cold-side rule

Once the boil ends and the wort begins to cool, treat every contact as sensitive. Keep hands, utensils, tubing, instruments and the fermenter clean and sanitized.

Follow the brew-day sequence

With grain, mashing lets malt enzymes convert starches into fermentable sugars. With malt extract, much of that work has already been done. Follow one recipe and one method instead of combining several protocols.

Boil the wort and add hops at the scheduled times. Cool it, transfer it into the sanitized fermenter, take the original gravity reading if required, pitch the yeast within its recommended temperature range, then close the fermenter.

Read next: IBU and Hops: Understanding Beer Bitterness

Let fermentation work

Keep the fermenter within the yeast manufacturer’s temperature range. Avoid repeated movement and unnecessary opening. Airlock activity varies with pressure and seal quality, so bubbles alone do not prove whether fermentation is active or complete.

Before packaging, respect the recipe timeline and confirm final gravity when instructed. Do not bottle beer while gravity is still falling: continued fermentation inside sealed bottles can create dangerous excess pressure.

Read next: Homebrew Fermentation: Time, Temperature and Signs

Record the measurements that matter

For a first batch, record volumes, key temperatures, hop-addition times, OG, FG and simple fermentation observations. Those notes explain most differences between the recipe and the finished beer.

OG estimates extract before fermentation. FG shows what remains afterward. Their difference estimates alcohol and apparent attenuation. IBU is a recipe estimate for bitterness, not a direct promise of how bitter the beer will taste.

In the homebrewing glossary: Original gravity.

Read next: Original Gravity, Final Gravity and ABV in Homebrewing

Avoid common first-batch mistakes

Do not improvise sanitizer dosage, return a sample to the fermenter, pitch yeast into wort that is too hot, or package on a fixed date without checking fermentation. These shortcuts create larger risks than a small calculation error.

Write down deviations instead of trying to correct several things at once. A clear record turns an imperfect batch into useful evidence for the next recipe.

Taste, record and improve the next batch

Taste the finished beer after carbonation and describe aroma, bitterness, sweetness, body and carbonation in plain language. Compare those notes with your measurements and recipe rather than judging the beer only as good or bad.

A useful final note

Record one thing to keep and one thing to change. That small feedback loop makes the second batch easier to plan and compare.
